scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants the power of immediate surroundings, then argues society shapes attitudes just as deeply; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: People's moods and opinions often shift depending on where they are and who is around them.
Some people argue that people's attitudes are determined more by their immediate situation than by society as a whole.
I agree that our surroundings strongly shape our attitudes, but I believe the wider society influences us just as deeply.

sections.role: Body 1 — The power of the immediate situation

sentences.text: First, our immediate surroundings clearly have a powerful effect on how we think and feel.
The people near us, and the pressures of the moment, can quickly change our behaviour.
For example, a calm person may become angry in a tense crowd or fearful in a dangerous place.
This shows that the situation right in front of us can shape our attitudes within minutes.
We often behave very differently at home, at work, and among strangers.
Immediate rewards and punishments push us to adjust our attitudes almost without thinking.
To this extent, our nearby situation is a strong force on our attitudes.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why society shapes us deeply

sentences.text: Second, however, the wider society shapes our attitudes just as deeply, if less visibly.
The values, language, and beliefs we absorb from our culture guide us everywhere we go.
Consider how ideas about right and wrong, learned from society, stay with us even when no one is watching.
Such deep beliefs show that society shapes the very person who then reacts to each situation.
Our reactions to an immediate situation are themselves guided by attitudes society taught us long ago.
Even rebellion against society is shaped by the society a person is rebelling against.
Society, then, works quietly beneath our reactions to every passing moment.
In conclusion, our immediate surroundings do strongly influence our day-to-day attitudes.
But the wider society shapes the deeper values through which we judge every situation.
In the end, our attitudes are best understood as the product of both the moment and the society behind it.
